description: Five visitor-accessible rounds in and around Las Vegas: the Strip-side Fazio at Wynn, the tropical spectacle of Bali Hai, the public TPC in Summerlin, Pete Dye's Wolf at Paiute, and the most historic course in town at Las Vegas National.
intro: Las Vegas is one of the easiest golf trips in America to plan: fly in, stay on the Strip, and play a genuinely great course within minutes of your hotel — no membership, no host, no connections required. The surprise is how much range the city offers, from a Tom Fazio layout you can walk to from a casino floor to a Pete Dye desert test half an hour out of town. The desert season is your friend — the best golf weather runs roughly October through May, when the mornings are cool and the afternoons are warm — so book early tee times, drink more water than you think you need, and pair a Strip course with a desert course for the full picture.

sections.heading: 1. Wynn Golf Club, Las Vegas Strip
paragraphs: The only golf course directly on the Las Vegas Strip sits behind Wynn and Encore on the north end of the boulevard, on the historic site of the Desert Inn course. Tom Fazio first turned the Desert Inn into Wynn Golf Club in 2005, then returned with his son Logan for a sweeping redesign that reopened in October 2019, rebuilding eight holes entirely and turning the 18th into a par 3 played over a dramatic waterfall. The result is a compact, theatrical par-70 with six par 3s, broad strategic fairways, more than 120 mature trees carried over from the Desert Inn days, and conditioning that holds up even in summer heat.

Wynn Golf Club is open to the public — any golfer can reserve a tee time by calling the Golf Concierge, with resort guests booking up to 90 days ahead and the general public within 30 days. There is no online booking, so call early for weekend mornings. Complimentary premium Callaway rental clubs are included in the green fee, and PGA-member caddies are available, so this is the easiest premium round in town to play light: fly in, walk off the casino floor, and play. Pair it with Bali Hai for a same-trip contrast between the Strip's two very different resort courses.

sections.heading: 2. Bali Hai Golf Club, Las Vegas Strip
paragraphs: At the south end of the Strip, beside Mandalay Bay, Bali Hai is the closest championship course to the boulevard — a public daily-fee layout you can reach by a short rideshare from most south-Strip hotels. Lee Schmidt and Brian Curley opened it in 2000 and committed fully to the tropical premise: 2,500 palms, 100,000 Balinese plants, seven acres of water, and black volcanic rock, all framed by Strip skyline views from multiple fairways. The par-71 layout plays 7,002 yards from the tips, and the par-3 island-green 16th — with an audience watching from the Cili restaurant patio — is one of the most photographed holes in the city.

Tee times are open to the public with no membership required, bookable through the club's website or by phone, and rental clubs and caddies are available if you travel without your bag. This is the best first round of a Vegas trip: it is walkable from the south Strip in spirit if not in summer heat, it plays in about four hours, and the spectacle is the point. Book it for your arrival day, when a morning flight and an afternoon tee time still leave you on the Strip by dinner.

sections.heading: 3. TPC Las Vegas, Summerlin
paragraphs: In Summerlin, about twenty minutes west of the Strip, TPC Las Vegas is the public half of the city's TPC pair — its sister course, TPC Summerlin, is private and hosts the Shriners Children's Open, while this one is open to anyone who books. Designed by Bobby Weed in consultation with World Golf Hall of Famer Raymond Floyd, it opened in 1996 as TPC at The Canyons and hosted the Shriners Hospitals for Children Open, the Bard Capital Challenge, and the Las Vegas Senior Classic from 1996 to 2006. The par-71, 7,016-yard layout — which TPC calls 'desert elegance' — is routed through a rugged canyon with views of Red Rock Canyon and the Las Vegas skyline, and the downhill par-5 18th finishes with the skyline as a backdrop.

Book through the TPC site or by phone, and treat this as the serious-golf round of the trip: it is a championship test with real tournament history, so play it on a fresh morning rather than after a late night. It pairs naturally with a second Summerlin-area round or with a drive out to Paiute the next day, since both sit on the west and northwest side of the valley. The course also offers blended tee yardages for men and women playing together, which makes it a good pick for a mixed-ability foursome.

sections.heading: 4. The Wolf at Las Vegas Paiute Golf Resort
paragraphs: The best pure golf in the Las Vegas area is a 25- to 30-minute drive northwest of the Strip, on Paiute tribal land beneath the Spring Mountains. Las Vegas Paiute Golf Resort holds three Pete Dye championship courses — Snow Mountain (1995), Sun Mountain (1996), and the Wolf — and the Wolf is the headliner: at 7,604 yards it is the longest course in Nevada, a par 72 of severe undulations, split fairways, and forced carries, with a near-island green on the par-3 15th that echoes Dye's famous 17th at TPC Sawgrass. There are no houses lining the fairways, no traffic noise, just open desert and mountain ridgelines — and GolfPass has ranked it the No. 1 public course in Nevada.

All three courses are public daily-fee with no membership required, and the resort offers multi-round packages, so plan a full day here rather than a single round: open on Snow Mountain or Sun Mountain, then take on the Wolf as the second round when you are warmed up. The Wolf is genuinely hard — pick a tee that keeps it playable rather than playing the tips for pride — and book morning tee times in the prime spring and fall season, when the valley is busiest. This is the round to build the trip around if you only get one desert test.

sections.heading: 5. Las Vegas National Golf Club
paragraphs: For history, nothing in town touches Las Vegas National. Designed by Bert Stamps, it opened in October 1961 as the Stardust Country Club and hosted the LPGA Championship — a women's major — in its very first year, with Hall of Famer Mickey Wright winning the inaugural edition. The Tournament of Champions was played here in 1967 and 1968, the Sahara Invitational ran here for years, and Tiger Woods shot 70 on this course in 1996 on his way to his first PGA Tour victory at the Las Vegas Invitational. The tree-lined, par-71 layout — rolling fairways, lakes, and greens guarded by palm, pine, and olive trees — feels like classic parkland golf, a world away from the desert courses, and parts of the course even served as a backdrop in the film Casino.

Las Vegas National is a public resort course less than ten minutes from the Strip, and it is the most affordable and most walkable-feeling round on this list, which makes it the ideal second or third round: a relaxed, historic morning before an afternoon flight home. Historical markers on the tee boxes tell the stories of the notable residents and moments tied to the course, so give yourself time to read them — the course doubles as a small museum of Las Vegas golf. Book it as the bookend to a trip that started with the spectacle of Bali Hai or Wynn.
